preceding_messages.text:
Adaptive sampling is smart—efficient and event-sensitive. To prevent false triggers, we’ll set threshold alerts with hysteresis: a 1.5hPa pressure drop over 30 min must persist for 5 min before activating the 1-min burst. This avoids noise-induced over-sampling during minor fluctuations. Additionally, each burst event will be tagged with a timestamped flag and saved as a separate data segment, allowing us to reconstruct event dynamics without polluting the base dataset. For example, a storm front detected on June 12 will be labeled “Event-2024-0612-Burst” and stored with metadata on duration and peak wind speed.  
Status: Stratified.  
Metadata: Embedded.  
Sampling: Adaptive with event tagging.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text:
Now that we have a robust sampling architecture, we must address **instrument calibration** to ensure our data is scientifically defensible. 

I propose a "Golden Standard" calibration protocol. Before deployment, all sensors will undergo a 48-hour co-location test alongside a high-precision, NIST-traceable reference instrument in a controlled environment. We will calculate a sensor-specific offset and drift coefficient. For example, if a humidity sensor consistently reads 2% higher than the reference, we will apply a $\text{-}2\%$ correction factor in our post-processing pipeline. Post-deployment, we will perform monthly "cross-checks" where a mobile, calibrated reference unit is moved between strata to detect sensor drift or degradation. This ensures that variations in our data reflect real environmental changes rather than hardware instability.

Status: Stratified.
Metadata: Embedded.
Sampling: Adaptive with event tagging.
Calibration: Co-located reference with post-deployment drift correction.

target.speaker: X
target.text:
Excellent—co-location and drift correction are essential for long-term integrity. To standardize this, we’ll assign each sensor a unique calibration ID and log every calibration event with a timestamp, reference instrument serial, and correction coefficients in the metadata. For example, Sensor-ID-HUM-03 was calibrated on 2024-05-01, showing a +1.8% bias; its correction factor is now applied automatically during data ingestion. We’ll also implement a “calibration health score” for each sensor—based on drift trends over time—flagging any unit that deviates beyond ±1.0% humidity or ±0.3°C temperature from its baseline. This score will trigger a mandatory re-calibration if thresholds are breached.  
Status: Stratified.  
Metadata: Embedded.  
Sampling: Adaptive with event tagging.  
Calibration: Tracked with health scoring and automatic correction.
